elements.quote: The objective of this systematic-review and meta-analysis was to compare the efficacy and safety of high-dose versus low-dose thromboprophylaxis in hospitalized patients with COVID-19.
elements.reason: The abstract explicitly identifies the report as a systematic review (and meta-analysis).

elements.quote: The objective of this systematic-review and meta-analysis was to compare the efficacy and safety of high-dose versus low-dose thromboprophylaxis in hospitalized patients with COVID-19.
elements.reason: The abstract states the main objective/review question explicitly.

elements.quote: MEDLINE and EMBASE were searched up to October 2021 for randomized clinical trials (RCTs) comparing high-dose with low-dose thromboprophylaxis in hospitalized adult patients with COVID-19.
elements.reason: The abstract specifies the key eligibility criteria (RCTs, high- vs low-dose thromboprophylaxis, hospitalized adult COVID-19 patients).

elements.quote: MEDLINE and EMBASE were searched up to October 2021
elements.reason: The abstract names the information sources (MEDLINE, EMBASE) and the date of the last search (October 2021).
The abstract does not mention any risk-of-bias assessment method; this is only described in the full text (revised Cochrane RoB tool).

elements.quote: The objective of this systematic-review and meta-analysis was to compare the efficacy and safety of high-dose versus low-dose thromboprophylaxis
elements.reason: Meta-analysis is identified as the synthesis approach, but the abstract does not describe how results were presented/synthesized (e.g., random-effects model, risk ratios).

elements.quote: A total of 5470 patients from 9 RCTs were included. Four trials included critically ill patients, four non-critically ill patients, and one included both.
elements.reason: The abstract reports the number of included studies (9 RCTs), participants (5470), and relevant study characteristics (illness severity distribution).

elements.quote: VTE occurred in 2.9% of patients on high-dose and in 5.7% of patients on low-dose thromboprophylaxis (relative risk [RR] 0.53; 95% confidence intervals [CIs], 0.41-0.69; I 2 = 0%; number needed to treat for an additional beneficial outcome, 22). Major bleeding occurred in 2.5% and 1.4% of patients, respectively (RR 1.78; 95% CI, 1.20-2.66; I 2 = 0%...). All-cause mortality did not differ between groups (RR 0.97; 95% CI, 0.75-1.26; I 2 = 47%).
elements.reason: The abstract presents results for the main outcomes (VTE, major bleeding, all-cause mortality) with effect estimates.

elements.quote: (relative risk [RR] 0.53; 95% confidence intervals [CIs], 0.41-0.69; I 2 = 0%; number needed to treat for an additional beneficial outcome, 22)
elements.reason: The abstract reports pooled summary estimates (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals for the meta-analysed outcomes.

elements.quote: The risk of VTE was significantly reduced by high-dose thromboprophylaxis in non-critically ill (RR 0.54; 95% CI, 0.35-0.86; I 2 = 0%), but not in critically ill patients (RR 0.69; 95% CI, 0.39-1.21; I 2 = 36%).
elements.reason: The abstract indicates the direction of effect and which group is favored (high-dose reduces VTE; increases major bleeding).
The abstract does not mention any limitations of the included evidence (e.g., risk of bias, open-label design, heterogeneity of definitions); limitations are discussed only in the full text.

elements.quote: In hospitalized patients with COVID-19, high-dose thromboprophylaxis is more effective than low-dose for the prevention of VTE but increases the risk of major bleeding.
elements.reason: The abstract provides a general interpretation of the results and their implications.
The abstract contains no funding statement; funding is only addressed in the full text ('There was no funding source for this study').
The abstract provides no registration name or registration number, and no registration information appears in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: The combination of systemic activation of coagulation, extensive pulmonary endotheliopathy and thromboinflammatory process caused by SARS-CoV2 results in an increased risk of thrombotic complications... Available data suggested that, despite pharmacologic thromboprophylaxis, there is a substantial residual risk of VTE and a non-negligible risk of bleeding events [3, 5]. In addition, it remains unclear whether prophylactic or higher doses of anticoagulants may reduce in-hospital mortality in COVID-19 patients [6, 7].
elements.reason: The Introduction describes current knowledge (VTE risk in COVID-19, observational study findings) and explicitly identifies uncertainties (unclear whether higher anticoagulant doses reduce mortality; conflicting RCT findings noted in text_4).

elements.quote: These observations left clinicians uncertain about the need for higher doses of thromboprophylaxis and resulted in heterogeneous indications from different guidance documents, in particular for critically ill patients.
elements.reason: The need for the review is explained by clinical uncertainty and inconsistent guidance, and the objective of the systematic review is stated (text_4: 'The objective of this systematic review and meta-analysis was to evaluate the pooled efficacy and safety of high-dose versus low-dose thromboprophylaxis...').
No similar existing systematic reviews are mentioned or cited anywhere in the retrieved evidence, so no explanation of need relative to prior reviews is required.

Although the disease mechanism (coagulation activation, endotheliopathy) is described, the proposed mechanism of action of the intervention itself (heparin/anticoagulant thromboprophylaxis) is not described in the retrieved evidence.

This is a review of a relatively simple pharmacological dose-comparison intervention (high- vs low-dose anticoagulation) in a single delivery context; no complex multi-component intervention or logic model requirement applies.

elements.quote: The objective of this systematic-review and meta-analysis was to compare the efficacy and safety of high-dose versus low-dose thromboprophylaxis in hospitalized patients with COVID-19.
elements.reason: An explicit objective statement is provided in the abstract, and reiterated in the text: 'The objective of this systematic review and meta-analysis was to evaluate the pooled efficacy and safety of high-dose versus low-dose thromboprophylaxis for VTE in hospitalized patients with COVID-19' (text_4).

elements.quote: The objective of this systematic-review and meta-analysis was to compare the efficacy and safety of high-dose versus low-dose thromboprophylaxis in hospitalized patients with COVID-19. ... The primary efficacy outcome was the occurrence of VTE and the primary safety outcome was major bleeding.
elements.reason: The planned comparison is stated in PICO form: population (hospitalized patients with COVID-19), intervention (high-dose thromboprophylaxis), comparator (low-dose thromboprophylaxis), and outcomes (VTE, major bleeding).

elements.quote: RCTs including hospitalized patients with objectively diagnosed SARS-CoV2 infection and comparing high-dose anticoagulation (experimental group) with low-dose anticoagulation (control group) were eligible. Studies with a non-randomised design or published in languages other than English were excluded.
elements.reason: Eligibility is well specified for design (RCTs only, non-randomised designs excluded), population (hospitalized adult patients with objectively diagnosed SARS-CoV2 infection), intervention (high-dose anticoagulation) and comparator (low-dose anticoagulation), with setting (hospitalized) implied. However, no follow-up requirements (and no outcome-based eligibility criteria) are stated as part of the inclusion/exclusion criteria, so the element is only partially fulfilled.

elements.quote: Studies with a non-randomised design or published in languages other than English were excluded.
elements.reason: A language restriction (English only) is explicitly stated. The search window (January 2020 to October 2021) implicitly limits dissemination dates but is not framed as an eligibility criterion, and no publication/report status criterion (e.g., published vs. preprint, peer-reviewed status) is specified.

elements.quote: Full-text articles excluded, with reasons (n = 1 – data reported in a previous RCTs)
elements.reason: Visible in the PRISMA flow diagram image (figure_5, attached to chunk text_9): the only full-text exclusion was because 'data reported in a previous RCTs' (duplicate reporting), not because outcomes were unmeasured or unreported. The text (text_6) confirms all nine included studies reported major bleeding and all-cause mortality, so no outcome-based exclusions occurred and the distinction is not applicable.

elements.quote: Sensitivity analyses were planned to compare the efficacy and safety of intermediate or therapeutic dose versus low-dose thromboprophylaxis, and of high-dose versus lowdose thromboprophylaxis in critically ill and non-critically ill COVID-19 patients. Critically ill patients included those admitted to ICU, patients requiring invasive mechanical ventilation, and patients with severe COVID-19 as defined by the study authors.
elements.reason: Synthesis groups are explicitly specified and defined: experimental (high-dose, i.e., intermediate or therapeutic dose, per text_4) versus control (low-dose), with subgroup/sensitivity analyses by dose category (intermediate vs therapeutic), illness severity (critically vs non-critically ill, with explicit definitions and a >75% patient threshold rule), intended-dose receipt, and symptomatic VTE. These groups directly link to the stated review objective of evaluating high-dose versus low-dose thromboprophylaxis (text_4).

Notable eligibility restrictions are imposed (RCT-only design, English-language-only publication), but no rationale or justification for these restrictions is provided anywhere in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: MEDLINE and EMBASE were searched from January 2020 up to October 2021
elements.reason: Coverage end date (October 2021) is given, but this is a coverage period rather than an explicit 'last searched' date for each source; only two sources are covered.

elements.quote: MEDLINE and EMBASE were searched from January 2020 up to October 2021
elements.reason: Database names (MEDLINE, EMBASE) and coverage dates are reported, but no search interface or platform is specified.
No registers, regulatory databases, or online repositories are reported as searched in the retrieved evidence.
No websites or search engines are reported as searched.
No organisations or manufacturers are reported as contacted.
No individuals are reported as contacted to identify studies.
No reference list searching is reported in the retrieved evidence.
No backward or forward citation searching is reported.

elements.quote: MEDLINE and EMBASE were searched from January 2020 up to October 2021 for RCTs comparing different regimens of venous thromboprophylaxis in hospitalized adult patients with COVID-19. The complete search strategy is shown in Supplementary Table 1.
elements.reason: Databases and date limits are reported and the full strategy is referenced in a supplementary table, but the actual search strings are not shown in the retrieved evidence and no other registers/websites are mentioned.

elements.quote: Studies with a non-randomised design or published in languages other than English were excluded.
elements.reason: Limits (date range, RCTs, English language) are described, but no explicit justification linking them to eligibility criteria is provided.
No citation of published search approaches, filters (e.g., Cochrane RCT filter), or adaptations is reported.
No evidence that natural-language processing or text-analysis tools were used; requirement does not apply.
No evidence that search translation tools were used; requirement does not apply.
No description of any validation of the search strategy is reported.
No peer review of the search strategy (e.g., PRESS) is reported.
No description of the conceptual structure of the search or its development is reported.

elements.quote: Two authors (EV and AP) independently screened the title and abstract of all records identified by the search.
elements.reason: The number of reviewers (two authors) is reported for title/abstract screening, but no reviewer count is specified for the full-text eligibility assessment stage; the flow diagram (figure_5, chunk text_9) shows full-text articles assessed (n=10) without attributing reviewers.

elements.quote: Two authors (EV and AP) independently screened the title and abstract of all records identified by the search.
elements.reason: Independent screening is explicitly stated for the title/abstract stage only; whether full-text reports were assessed independently is not reported.

elements.quote: Any disagreement was resolved through discussion between the review authors or involving a third review author (MDN).
elements.reason: The study search and selection section describes the disagreement resolution process, including escalation to a third review author (MDN).
No evidence that eligibility information was sought from or confirmed with study investigators; the retrieved text contains no mention of contacting authors.

elements.quote: Studies with a non-randomised design or published in languages other than English were excluded.
elements.reason: Non-English publications were excluded by eligibility criteria, so no translation of abstracts or full articles was required.
No automation tools are mentioned anywhere in the retrieved selection process description; screening was performed manually by two authors.
No externally derived classifiers were used; all 224 identified records were screened manually, as reflected in the methods text and flow diagram.
No internally derived classifiers or machine-learning tools are reported; selection was conducted by human reviewers only.
No machine-learning prioritisation tools or stopping rules are described in the retrieved evidence.
No crowdsourcing platforms are mentioned in the retrieved evidence.
No previously screened datasets used to eliminate records are reported; all records came from the authors' own MEDLINE and EMBASE search.

elements.quote: The primary efficacy outcome was the occurrence of any symptomatic or incidental VTE. Secondary efficacy outcomes were all-cause mortality, acute myocardial infarction, acute ischemic stroke, acute peripheral arterial ischemic events, symptomatic or incidental deep vein thrombosis (DVT), and symptomatic or incidental pulmonary embolism (PE). The primary safety outcome was major bleeding as defined by the authors, while the secondary safety outcomes were clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding and heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.
elements.reason: All outcome domains sought (VTE, DVT, PE, all-cause mortality, arterial thrombotic events, major bleeding, clinically relevant non-major bleeding, HIT) are comprehensively listed with a primary/secondary hierarchy, but definitions are incomplete: major bleeding is deferred to study authors ('as defined by the authors'), and clinically relevant non-major bleeding and HIT are not defined at the review level; Table 1 only reports heterogeneous study-specific definitions.

No time frame of measurement is specified for any outcome domain; the methods only list 'follow-up duration' as an extracted data item, and follow-up windows (21-30 days) appear only as study characteristics in Table 1, not as defined measurement time points per outcome.
The manuscript nowhere states whether all results compatible with each outcome domain in each study (all measures, time points, analyses) were sought.

The manuscript does not indicate that only a subset of compatible results was collected within outcome domains, so the conditional requirement to describe a result-selection process is not triggered by the available evidence.
No changes to outcome-domain inclusion, definitions, or importance (e.g., protocol amendments) are reported anywhere in the retrieved text, so there is nothing to report with rationale.
No changes to processes for selecting results within outcome domains are reported in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: The primary efficacy outcome was the occurrence of any symptomatic or incidental VTE. ... The primary safety outcome was major bleeding as defined by the authors
elements.reason: The outcomes considered most important are identifiable through the designation of primary efficacy (VTE) and primary safety (major bleeding) outcomes, but no explicit rationale for this prioritisation is provided.

elements.quote: Two authors (EV and AP) independently extracted the following data: study characteristics (e.g., number of included patients, health-care setting), patient characteristics (e.g., age, sex, presence of comorbidities, disease severity), anticoagulant regimens in both experimental and control groups (e.g., type, dose, and duration of anticoagulation), number of patients who experienced the outcome of interest, and follow-up duration.
elements.reason: The methods list the variables sought (study and patient characteristics, anticoagulant regimens, outcomes, follow-up), with outcome definitions further detailed in Table 1.
No explicit description of assumptions made about missing or unclear study information is reported in the retrieved evidence.
No tool for determining which data items to collect is mentioned; use of such a tool is optional and no evidence indicates one was used.

elements.quote: The risk of bias was independently evaluated by two authors (EV and AP) with the revised Cochrane risk-ofbias tool for randomized trials [15].
elements.reason: The tool used is explicitly named (revised Cochrane risk-of-bias tool for randomized trials, i.e., RoB 2) with a reference.
The domains or items assessed by the revised Cochrane risk-of-bias tool are not described anywhere in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: Four RCTs had an overall high risk of bias and five RCTs presented some concerns regarding the overall risk of bias (Fig. 2).
elements.reason: An overall risk-of-bias judgement was made and reported (with Fig. 2 summary), but the rules used to derive the overall judgement are not reported.
No adaptations to the risk-of-bias tool are reported or suggested; the standard revised Cochrane tool was used.
No newly developed risk-of-bias tool was used; an existing validated tool was applied.

elements.quote: The risk of bias was independently evaluated by two authors (EV and AP) with the revised Cochrane risk-ofbias tool for randomized trials [15]. Any disagreement was resolved through discussion between the review authors or involving a third review author (MDN).
elements.reason: Number of reviewers (two), independent assessment, and disagreement-resolution procedure (discussion or third author) are all reported.
No processes for obtaining or confirming risk-of-bias information from study investigators are reported, and there is no indication such contact was attempted.
No automation tools for risk-of-bias assessment are mentioned; the assessment was performed manually by two authors.

elements.quote: Pooled risk ratios (RRs) with corresponding 95% confidence intervals (CIs) and prediction intervals (PIs) were calculated using a random-effects model.
elements.reason: The Methods specify risk ratios (with 95% CIs and prediction intervals) as the effect measure for the binary outcomes, and additionally pooled absolute risk reductions and NNTB/NNTH for primary outcomes; results sections consistently report RRs for all outcomes.

No thresholds or ranges for interpreting the magnitude of effect sizes (e.g., what constitutes a small/clinically important RR) and their rationale are reported; the I2 ranges given relate to heterogeneity, not effect size interpretation.

elements.quote: To help the interpretation of the data, we also expressed the results in absolute terms, i.e., the number of events that would occur in 1000 patients receiving high-dose thromboprophylaxis, using the observed risk in the low-dose group and the pooled relative risk with its 95% CIs.
elements.reason: The methods describe re-expressing the pooled relative risk as absolute event numbers per 1000 patients, i.e., conversion to another effect measure.
The choice of risk ratio as the effect measure is stated but no justification for choosing it (over e.g., odds ratio) is provided.

elements.quote: Sensitivity analyses were planned to compare the efficacy and safety of intermediate or therapeutic dose versus low-dose thromboprophylaxis, and of high-dose versus low-dose thromboprophylaxis in critically ill and non-critically ill COVID-19 patients... We included a study in one of the subgroups above if more than 75% of patients in that study fulfilled these criteria. Furthermore, post hoc sensitivity analyses were performed including only RCTs in which patients received the intended high-dose or low-dose thromboprophylaxis and to evaluate the efficacy of high-dose versus low-dose thromboprophylaxis in symptomatic VTE.
elements.reason: The methods describe which studies were eligible for each synthesis: main meta-analysis of high- vs low-dose, subgroup syntheses (intermediate vs therapeutic dose; critically vs non-critically ill) with an explicit decision rule (>75% of patients meeting criteria), and post hoc sensitivity analyses restricted to RCTs with intended dosing or symptomatic VTE data. Study intervention characteristics were also tabulated (Table 1) to support assignment to syntheses.

elements.quote: To help the interpretation of the data, we also expressed the results in absolute terms, i.e., the number of events that would occur in 1000 patients receiving high-dose thromboprophylaxis, using the observed risk in the low-dose group and the pooled relative risk with its 95% CIs.
elements.reason: Some data preparation/conversion methods are described (converting relative risks to absolute terms per 1000 patients, subgroup classification criteria, handling of a combined venous/arterial outcome), but there is no description of handling missing summary statistics or other data preparation steps.

elements.quote: The main characteristics of the included RCTs are listed in Table 1.
elements.reason: Table 1 is described as presenting study characteristics (population, doses, regimens, definitions, follow-up), and its content is shown in table_0/table_1.

elements.quote: Heterogeneity among the included studies was evaluated by visual inspection of forest plots and the DerSimonian-Laird estimator
elements.reason: Forest plots are described as graphical displays of results (also Fig. 3 with detailed legend in table_2), and funnel plots for publication bias are mentioned in text_6.

elements.quote: Therapeutic vs Low-dose heparin ... Intermediate vs Low-dose heparin ... Critically-ill patients
elements.reason: The forest plot (Fig. 3) groups studies by dose comparison and indicates critical illness status, but the Methods text does not explicitly describe the basis for ordering or grouping studies within tables or graphs.
Only standard displays (forest plots, funnel plots, risk-of-bias summary, PRISMA flow diagram) are used; no non-standard graphs requiring rationale.

elements.quote: R Core Team (2019) R: A language and environment for statistical computing. R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria.
elements.reason: R is cited in the reference list, implying the software used, but the Methods section never explicitly states which software/package was used for the meta-analysis, and no package names or versions are given.
A meta-analysis was performed (pooled RRs reported), so the requirement for describing an alternative synthesis when meta-analysis was not possible does not apply.

elements.quote: Over the last months, several studies showed that hospitalized patients with COVID-19 have a high risk of VTE despite receiving standard pharmacological thromboprophylaxis [3]. ... Observational studies reported promising results in terms of survival rate and respiratory failure reduction among patients receiving highdose anticoagulation, however, there was a concerning signal for an increased risk of bleeding complications [6, 7]. Based on these preliminary reports, international guidelines suggested, with a very low certainty, the administration of standard venous thromboprophylaxis in all COVID-19 hospitalized patients... The results of this metaanalysis support a greater efficacy from high-doses of thromboprophylaxis...
elements.reason: The Discussion interprets the meta-analysis results in the context of prior observational studies, guidelines, and other RCT evidence (e.g., Goligher, Lawler).

elements.quote: There are some limitations which warrant discussion. First, the dose and duration of anticoagulant regimens varied widely across the studies... Second, the open-label design of all included trials represents a potential limitation and ascertainment bias cannot be excluded for VTE and major bleeding. Third, outcome definitions varied across trials... and all studies were underpowered to show differences in VTE or bleeding events.
